Health Squared

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Your Medical Aid gives you 2 weeks notice that they're closing down, but you need dialysis 3 times a week. How did it come to this?

Unique Selling Point:
Case study Sharon Waison (30) needs dialysis treatment 3 x per week: Monday, Wednesday and Friday. She was diagnosed with Lupus at the age of 10 and went into renal failure in 2015, starting dialysis a year later. She is a dependent on her mother's hospital plan from Health Squared. They belonged to Resolution Health for 10 years before they merged with Spectramed to form Health Squared. Her treatment at Fourways Life Hospital costs about R30 000 per month. When Health Squared told them she would no longer be covered as of the 31st of August, she panicked. They were advised to join another medical aid, but were warned that a waiting period of weeks or months would apply. Her nephrologist Dr Rachael de Zeeuw told Sharon she doesn't have a week. Without dialysis she will die.

Summary:
Health Squared applied for voluntary liquidation as a result of an acute solvency crisis brought about by a rapidly dwindling membership and an above-average proportion of pensioners. Since its formation in 2019, Health Squared has failed to meet the industry’s required 25% solvency ratio — a measure of its ability to pay claims. The scheme informed its almost 24,000 members on August 18 that no claims for health services after August 31 would be paid.
In a letter to members, principal officer, Elias Mabena, said the board of trustees of Health Squared Medical Scheme “had resolved to approach the High Court in terms of Section 51 of the Medical Schemes Act for leave to apply for the voluntary winding up of the scheme in the interest of its members. The primary driver of the financial deterioration of the scheme during 2020 and 2021 was high Covid-19 claims expenditure. The scheme was particularly impacted relative to medical scheme industry norms due to its older than average age profile. As at July 31, it had an average beneficiary age of 49.7 years, which is 16.1 years higher than the medical scheme industry average of 33.6 years.
The bombshell decision was in defiance of industry regulator the Council for Medical Schemes’ (CMS) intention to appoint a curator to oversee the running of the scheme to protect its members. CMS was aware Health Squared's insolvency level, and had flagged it in their last Annual Report. CMS told everyone not find another medical aid while the Council negotiated with industry players for favourable terms. But at the last minute - 10.00pm on 31 August they announced that negotiations had been unsuccessful.
That left members left high and dry, scrambling to find alternative medical cover. They will more than likely be forced to endure waiting periods, even for the 126 conditions that fall under Prescribed Minimum Benefits.

Further information:
This weekend Judge Allyson Crutchfield ruled that more than 50 Health Squared medical scheme members undergoing dialysis will have their treatment and medication covered by the close-to-insolvent scheme until the end of this month, or until they join another scheme.
That was made an order of the Johannesburg high court at the weekend. The ruling is a lifeline not only to the scheme’s 54 dialysis and kidney transplant patients, but to all members “experiencing grave, life-threatening risks”.
In terms of the order, Health Squared may not apply for liquidation before September 27, and remains an active scheme until a liquidation order is finalised.

There are also reports that in the months leading up to its demise, troubled medical scheme Health Squared blew millions of rands of members’ contributions on marketing campaigns, exorbitant trustee fees and other non-essential items.
A trove of documents attached in the scheme’s high court application for voluntary liquidation, as well as further documents leaked from the Council for Medical Schemes (CMS), the regulator of the medical aid industry, show that the company had operated in breach of solvency requirements and was consistently overspending on non-healthcare items.
A Durban broker reports she attended a Health Squared training and accreditation workshop held at the Oyster Box Hotel in June.
While she has been inundated with requests from people looking for a new medical aid, she reports that some received unsolicited SMS's from Sizwe Hosmed scheme offering cover with no waiting period. Who leaked the Health Squared database?

Thousands of people have been left stressed and anxious and with no medical cover for the next few months. What went wrong and who is to blame?


Extra Budget Items:
Possible airfare and accommodation. Both Wendy Knowler and Shenaaz Dramat are in Cape Town. While Zoom interviews are possible, it may be better to have the presenter in situ?
Karen Howard is in Durban - an extra half-day for a cameraman.

Script:


HEALTH SQUARED


V/O: It’s been a month of high drama for a small medical scheme called Health Squared. They promised “Complete cover from every angle” but failed to mention they were in financial trouble. Without warning they applied for voluntary liquidation in August, and 14 000 members and 23 000 dependents were given two weeks to find another medical scheme.

Link: For those of us lucky enough to have private health insurance, it’s one of the first things we budget for. But what happens when your medical scheme suddenly closes down and you’re no longer covered?

Sharon: If I don’t do dialysis, within a week I’m dead. That is my reality.

V/O: It’s sunrise on a Monday morning and Sharon Waison is being dropped off by her mother Vanessa, for treatment at Life Fourways hospital in Johannesburg. She’s in end stage renal failure, so this routine is repeated three times a week, without fail.

Sharon: I was diagnosed with systemic lupus at the age of 10. I never had a proper childhood I would say.

Vanessa: So when Sharon was diagnosed with lupus, the doctor did call me in and said that her kidneys could go into renal failure down the line. And before I know it she’s 30 years old, and her kidneys are functioning at 0%. And with dialysis at 2%.

V/O: Sharon’s been waiting 5 years for a kidney transplant. She used to be a professional gamer but her fragile health forced her to retire.

Sharon: Last year March I actually landed up dying. They had to resuscitate me.

Masa: What happened?

00:10:54 I bled internally, from complications from lupus and kidney failure.

V/O: Sharon’s nephrologist is Dr Rachael de Zeeuw.

Rachael: She had a lupus flare and she had inflammation of the blood vessels in her colon. She essentially just bled out and she needed huge volumes of fluid and blood resuscitation in the intensive care unit. And all those massive fluid shifts put a lot of strain on her heart.

Masa: So in this household medical aid must be a non-negotiable.

Vanessa: Non-negotiable.

Masa: How long have you been on medical aid?

Vanessa: So with Health Squared we’ve been on since 2007.

V/O They were members of Resolution Health which merged with Spectramed in 2018 to form Health Squared.

Every Monday, Wednesday and Friday, Sharon has a 4-hour dialysis session.

Vanessa: Health Squared has covered the dialysis and that comes to about, I think 30, 35000 a month.

Masa: Did you even know Health Squared was in trouble?

Vanessa: No! No! We received an email on the 18th of August, telling us from the 1st of September, we need to find a new medical scheme. That gives you eight working days. I mean, how can they do that?

Doctor: Sharon unfortunately has got no residual kidney function left at all. She wouldn’t survive two weeks without dialysis. In fact, I don’t even know if she would survive one.

V/O: According to Health Squared administered by Agility, high Covid-19 related claims, an ageing member profile, and a high proportion of pensioners had left the scheme with less than 3% reserves by July this year. A solvency ratio is the measure of a scheme’s ability to pay claims.

Mark: In 2019 they had a solvency ratio of just under 20%, which is outside the requirements of the Council for Medical Schemes. Solvency ratios have to run at 25%.

V/O: Mark Hyman serves on the Fraud, Waste and Abuse Advisory Committee of the CMS.

Mark: Council for Medical Schemes became aware of this and as far back as 2019 had been negotiating with Health Squared to get their solvency ratio increased. By the end of December 2021 the solvency ratio of Health Squared was at 17.3%.

Link: Many members have asked why the Council for Medical Schemes didn’t see this coming? Well they did.
Then why didn’t they do something about it? They say they tried.
But the Board of Health Squared resisted the appointment of a statutory manager last year, an intervention that could have helped to turn things around.

V/O: A statutory manager takes control of a Scheme to steer it back to financial solvency.

Sharon and other members in renal failure got a lifeline on the 4th of September, when the court ordered Health Squared to cover treatment for 54 dialysis patients and members suffering from grave, life-threatening risks until the end of September.

But Health Squared ignored that order, when the access graft to Sharon’s femoral artery became blocked.

Sharon: I was on the dialysis machine and it just started beeping.

V/O: She needed surgery to open the graft, but the hospital pre-authorization was rejected by Health Squared.
33:21
Vanessa: I was shaking and I was in tears because there’s a court order in place. So that was on the Friday. Saturday morning I then get a call from Fourways Life Hospital. She says, I’m sorry, unfortunately we are no longer accepting Health Squared members.

Masa: What does that mean?

Vanessa: We can’t go there on Monday for Sharon’s operation. That’s what it means.

Rachael: What I would equate it to is if you’re scuba diving and you’re sitting at the bottom at 30 meters, and someone takes your regulator away and says good luck!

Masa: Oh no!

Rachael: It’s her lifeline. And she requires it three times a week and someone has just taken it away from her.

Vanessa: And I said to the lady do you know that there is a court order in place? She says yes I know, but we are not accepting Health Squared members.

V/O: Life Healthcare denied this saying that at no stage was the patient in question refused admission to, or treatment at, Life Fourways Hospital. Our standard process was followed and we informed the patient that as the authorisation was declined by Health Squared, a private admission was necessary.

Link: But that’s not what Carte Blanche was told when our producer called Life Fourways the same day. From this recording it’s pretty clear that all Health Squared members would no longer be treated at the hospital, unless they have a new medical aid or pay cash.

Desiree: So Life Healthcare has sent communication through to the hospitals that we will no longer be having any dealings with Health Squared. So all their patients, either they present us with a new medical aid, or we do a pre-estimate for them.

Kate: Right.

Desiree: So it’s a Life Healthcare decision, it’s not a hospital decision.

Mark: The financial implication alone would have precluded her from having that procedure. Where does a young girl of 30, unemployed because of her condition, find the money? So we launched that court application.

V/O: Mark Hyman runs a service called MediCheck, which has set up a Health Squared Hotline helping members in this exact predicament.

Mark: And we submitted to the urgent court in Johannesburg an urgent application to ensure that an authorization was provided by 2:00pm that afternoon, and that the hospital agreed to admit the patient into the hospital. That authorization was approved at 1:50 on Sunday afternoon.

V/O: The Court has placed Health Squared under the provisional curatorship of Joe Seolane. He’s been investigating what went wrong.

Joe: The last AGM was for the year 2020. Even in that year the Scheme had made over 100 million losses. In 2021 the death spiral starts coming through that says you are starting to spend all the money you receive in contributions in paying claims. And you are left with nothing to pay for the non-healthcare costs.

Link: From 2019 to 2022 Health Squared spent R90 million on marketing, to try and promote the brand. But it didn’t work. Instead of attracting new members, they lost over 9000 members. And along with them went their monthly premiums.

V/O: He also believes the Board of Trustees played a significant role in the Scheme’s demise.
Joe: For a scheme of this size to spend 3.2 million per annum on Trustees, to me it is way above what the market would do for a similar size with similar challenges.

V/O: Seoloane is determined to do a thorough investigation before the Scheme is liquidated.

Joe: You can’t save it now. What you need to do is to give it a decent winding up. That does not become so urgent to wind up to cover up.

V/O: Last week, Sharon was accepted as a member of Discovery Health and is still hoping to find a suitable match for a kidney transplant.

Sharon: At the end of the day, I’m still grateful for life. You know, I could have not been here and I got a second chance.

metadata.Summary: Health Squared applied for voluntary liquidation as a result of an acute solvency crisis brought about by a rapidly dwindling membership and an above-average proportion of pensioners. Since its formation in 2019, Health Squared has failed to meet the industry’s required 25% solvency ratio — a measure of its ability to pay claims. The scheme informed its almost 24,000 members on August 18 that no claims for health services after August 31 would be paid. In a letter to members, principal officer, Elias Mabena, said the board of trustees of Health Squared Medical Scheme “had resolved to approach the High Court in terms of Section 51 of the Medical Schemes Act for leave to apply for the voluntary winding up of the scheme in the interest of its members. The primary driver of the financial deterioration of the scheme during 2020 and 2021 was high Covid-19 claims expenditure. The scheme was particularly impacted relative to medical scheme industry norms due to its older than average age profile. As at July 31, it had an average beneficiary age of 49.7 years, which is 16.1 years higher than the medical scheme industry average of 33.6 years. The bombshell decision was in defiance of industry regulator the Council for Medical Schemes’ (CMS) intention to appoint a curator to oversee the running of the scheme to protect its members. CMS was aware Health Squared's insolvency level, and had flagged it in their last Annual Report. CMS told everyone not find another medical aid while the Council negotiated with industry players for favourable terms. But at the last minute - 10.00pm on 31 August they announced that negotiations had been unsuccessful. That left members left high and dry, scrambling to find alternative medical cover. They will more than likely be forced to endure waiting periods, even for the 126 conditions that fall under Prescribed Minimum Benefits.
metadata.Further information: This weekend Judge Allyson Crutchfield ruled that more than 50 Health Squared medical scheme members undergoing dialysis will have their treatment and medication covered by the close-to-insolvent scheme until the end of this month, or until they join another scheme. That was made an order of the Johannesburg high court at the weekend. The ruling is a lifeline not only to the scheme’s 54 dialysis and kidney transplant patients, but to all members “experiencing grave, life-threatening risks”. In terms of the order, Health Squared may not apply for liquidation before September 27, and remains an active scheme until a liquidation order is finalised. There are also reports that in the months leading up to its demise, troubled medical scheme Health Squared blew millions of rands of members’ contributions on marketing campaigns, exorbitant trustee fees and other non-essential items. A trove of documents attached in the scheme’s high court application for voluntary liquidation, as well as further documents leaked from the Council for Medical Schemes (CMS), the regulator of the medical aid industry, show that the company had operated in breach of solvency requirements and was consistently overspending on non-healthcare items. A Durban broker reports she attended a Health Squared training and accreditation workshop held at the Oyster Box Hotel in June. While she has been inundated with requests from people looking for a new medical aid, she reports that some received unsolicited SMS's from Sizwe Hosmed scheme offering cover with no waiting period. Who leaked the Health Squared database? Thousands of people have been left stressed and anxious and with no medical cover for the next few months. What went wrong and who is to blame?
